newsitem.title: JAPAN: Oriental Land shares hinge on new Disney park.
newsitem.headline: Oriental Land shares hinge on new Disney park.

text.p: Oriental Land Co Ltd, operator of Tokyo Disneyland, will make its share debut on Wednesday and is likely to be the last major listing on the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) this year.

The power of the globally known "Disney" brand is expected to attract Japanese investors, specially individuals, but analysts said the future level of Oriental Land's stock depends on the fate of a new theme park it plans to open in 2001, called "Tokyo Disney Sea".

Since Oriental Land, which earns 97 percent of its revenue from Tokyo Disneyland, is expected to see a limited increase in the number of people visiting the existing park in the near future, its profits depend on whether it succeeds in attracting more visitors by opening the new theme park, they said.
"The outlook of the company will depend on whether the new theme park will succeed or not," said Tsuyoshi Taniguchi, analyst at Nikko Research Center.
In the last business year that ended in March, 1996, a record number of 16.986 million people visited Tokyo Disneyland.

Analysts said the number was surprising when compared with the number of Japanese tourists abroad in the same year, 15 million people, which reflected the recent domestic fashion for travelling to foreign countries.

A spokesman for Oriental Land said the end of the long-lasting popular "Tokyo Disneyland Electrical Parade" in the summer of 1996 galvanised people who wanted to see the last parade. A new parade, "Disney's FANTILLUSION!", also gained popularity.
Analysts said the number of visitors was likely to hover around 17 million for a few years, but added that too little information has been released to predict the popularity of the future theme park.

Oriental Land, which is tight-lipped about its outlook ahead of the listing on the Tokyo stock exchange, has not unveiled details of the new theme park, which will include attractions featuring what it describes as "fascinating harbours" and "brave navigation".
Oriental Land reached a basic agreement with Walt Disney Co in May on the new park and it would take 18 months to draw up a concrete plan for "Tokyo Disney Sea", a company spokesman said.
"It doesn't mean that Oriental Land has no promising future. But there are too many unknown factors," said Hidekazu Umemura, analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities & Economics Inc.
The spokesman said the scale of the new park is likely to be almost the same as Tokyo Disneyland's 46 hectares.

Umemura said the focus was on whether Oriental Land has scope to reduce costs after it opens "Tokyo Disney Sea", as its overall costs for employees, food and character goods are expected to double after opening the park.
But the total number of visitors is unlikely to rise on the same scale after the park opens, he said.

Ninety-five percent of visitors to Tokyo Disneyland every year are so-called "repeaters", people who have visited the park more than one time. That makes it difficult to boost the number of visitors dramatically only by opening a new theme park, analysts said.

Umemura expected the share price of Oriental Land to hover between about 7,000 yen ($62) and 9,000 yen ($80) until it becomes clear how much premium can be added to the share after the second theme park is opened.

In late November, the weighted average price for Oriental Land at an auction of 11.5 million shares was set at 8,368 yen ($74). The company later announced that the initial public offering price for another 11.5 million shares was set at 8,050 yen ($71). The company's shares will be listed on the first section of the TSE on December 11.
